title: Memory & CLAUDE.md
description: Teach Claude your project once, so it remembers every session.

lessons.title: Meet CLAUDE.md
lessons.description: The file Claude reads at the start of every session.

theory.title: A briefing that loads itself
theory.body:
Each new session starts with a blank conversation. `CLAUDE.md` fixes that: it's a plain **Markdown** file that Claude Code **loads automatically** at the start of every session, so Claude already knows your commands when you ask it to run the tests.

Write **concrete, actionable** lines (`run pnpm test`), not vague advice (`write good code`).
theory.code:
# CLAUDE.md

## Commands
- npm run dev: start the dev server
- npm test: run unit tests

## Conventions
- TypeScript strict mode; no `any`
- Use named exports

theory.title: Where it lives
theory.body:
The project file is named exactly `CLAUDE.md` (capital letters) and sits in your **project root**, the top folder of the repo, next to files like `package.json`.

**Commit it to git** so it travels with the repo and your whole team gets the same instructions. Kip keeps his tucked inside his shell, so he never forgets how to run the tests.
theory.code:
my-app/
├── src/
├── package.json
└── CLAUDE.md      ← project memory

exercises.prompt: When does Claude Code read your project's CLAUDE.md?
options: Automatically at the start of each session
exercises.explanation: CLAUDE.md files are loaded into context automatically when a session starts.

exercises.prompt: What format is CLAUDE.md?
exercises.explanation: It's ordinary Markdown, so headings and bullet lists keep it readable for you and Claude.

exercises.prompt: Match the problem to how CLAUDE.md solves it.

pairs.left: Claude uses npm, you use pnpm

exercises.explanation: Anything you would otherwise repeat every session belongs in CLAUDE.md, because it loads automatically.

exercises.prompt: Which CLAUDE.md entry is more useful?
options: Write good code and be careful.
Run `pnpm test --filter api` for API tests; they need `docker compose up db` first.
exercises.explanation: Concrete, actionable instructions help, while vague advice adds noise.

exercises.prompt: Why commit the project CLAUDE.md to git?
options: Claude Code only reads committed files
Your whole team gets the same project instructions
exercises.explanation: A checked-in CLAUDE.md shares commands and conventions with everyone working in the repo.

exercises.prompt: Complete the project memory file's name and location.
exercises.explanation: Claude Code looks for a file named exactly CLAUDE.md at the project root, so the name and location both matter.
exercises.hint: The memory file is named after Claude, in capitals, and sits at the root.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when you start a session in a repo with CLAUDE.md.
steps: You run claude in the project
Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md into context
You ask Claude to run the tests
Claude uses the test command from CLAUDE.md
exercises.explanation: Because memory loads at startup, Claude already knows your commands when you ask.

lessons.title: Bootstrap with /init
lessons.description: Let Claude write the first draft for you.

theory.title: Don't start from a blank page
theory.body:
Run `/init` inside a session and Claude **analyzes your codebase** (package files, configs, folder structure) and writes a starter `CLAUDE.md`. Since `/init` is a slash command, start a session with `claude` first.

Notice the two prompts below: `$` is your normal terminal, `>` is inside Claude.

theory.title: Then make it yours
theory.body:
Treat the result as a **first draft**. `/init` can detect what's visible in code, like build and test commands and folder structure. It can't know your team's **tribal knowledge**: the unwritten rules people only learn by asking, like `staging DB resets nightly` or `ask before touching billing`.

So: run `/init` → review the draft → delete fluff and add gotchas → commit `CLAUDE.md` to git.

exercises.prompt: What does /init base its CLAUDE.md on?
options: A generic template, identical for every repo
exercises.explanation: /init reads your project's files to describe its commands, structure, and conventions.

exercises.prompt: /init generated a CLAUDE.md. What should you do next?
options: Delete it; generated files are useless
Review it and add knowledge only your team has
exercises.explanation: The draft captures what's visible in code; you add what isn't, like deploy quirks.

exercises.prompt: Who adds what to CLAUDE.md?
exercises.explanation: /init finds what's in the code; team knowledge and preferences come from you.

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to improve your existing CLAUDE.md. Which request is better?
options: Review @CLAUDE.md: remove anything obvious from the code, and add our test command (pnpm test) and the rule that migrations live in db/migrations/.
exercises.explanation: Specific additions and removals produce a tighter memory file.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to set up project memory.
steps: cd into the project and run claude
Add team gotchas and remove fluff
exercises.explanation: Generating, refining and then committing means the team shares a draft that has been checked by a human.

exercises.prompt: At your normal terminal, inside the project folder, start Claude Code so you can run /init next.
exercises.hint: Slash commands only work inside a session; start one with the tool name: cl…
exercises.explanation: Slash commands like /init only exist inside an interactive session, which you open with claude.

exercises.prompt: You're inside a session. Type the slash command that generates a starter CLAUDE.md for this project.
exercises.explanation: /init reads your codebase and drafts a CLAUDE.md, so you start from real project facts instead of a blank page.

lessons.title: Project vs User Memory
lessons.description: Team rules in the repo, personal rules in your home.

theory.title: Two places, two audiences
theory.body:
**Project memory**: `./CLAUDE.md` in the repo (`./` means "this folder"). Shared with your team through git: build commands, architecture, conventions.

**User memory**: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. `~` is your home folder and `.claude` is a hidden settings folder inside it. It applies to **all your projects**, but only for you: personal preferences like answer style.

Same file name, different folder. Both load automatically.
theory.code:
./CLAUDE.md            # project: shared via git
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md    # user: all your projects, only you

theory.title: Imports keep it tidy
theory.body: A CLAUDE.md can pull in other files by writing `@` followed by the path, no space. Point at existing docs instead of copying them, so there's one source of truth.
theory.code:
Project overview: @README.md
Git workflow: @docs/git-workflow.md
PR process: see @CONTRIBUTING.md

theory.title: Open them with /memory
theory.body: Inside a session, the slash command `/memory` lists your memory files (project and user) and opens the one you pick in your editor.

exercises.prompt: Where does user memory, which applies to all your projects, live?
exercises.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is your personal memory, loaded in every project.

exercises.prompt: Match the instruction to the right memory file.
exercises.explanation: Repo facts help every teammate so they go in project memory, while personal taste stays in user memory.

exercises.prompt: Your teammate shouldn't get your personal "answer in Spanish" preference. Where does it go?
exercises.explanation: User memory isn't in the repo, so it only affects you.

exercises.prompt: Your 400-line CONTRIBUTING.md already explains the PR process. How should CLAUDE.md use it?
exercises.explanation: An import keeps one source of truth instead of a stale duplicate.

exercises.prompt: Complete the paths for both memory files.
exercises.explanation: Both use the same filename, so the folder (./ or ~/.claude/) is what decides whether it is shared or personal.
exercises.hint: Both files share one name; only the folder in front changes.

exercises.prompt: Import your existing docs into CLAUDE.md.
exercises.explanation: @path inside CLAUDE.md imports another file, so you reuse existing docs instead of duplicating them.
exercises.hint: Imports in CLAUDE.md use the same prefix as file references in prompts.

exercises.prompt: Inside a session, type the slash command that opens your memory files (project or user CLAUDE.md) in your editor.
exercises.hint: / + the word for what CLAUDE.md is: /mem…
exercises.explanation: /memory lets you pick a memory file (like ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) and opens it in your editor.

theory.title: High signal only
theory.body:
Great CLAUDE.md content is **specific and repeatedly useful**. Group it under three headings:

**Commands**: build, test, lint, run a single test.

**Conventions**: naming, file layout, preferred libraries.

**Gotchas**: the weird stuff that trips people up.

Skip things Claude can see in the code anyway. Every line is loaded into context in **every** session, so keep it short.
theory.code:
# CLAUDE.md

## Commands
- pnpm test: unit tests
- pnpm lint --fix: lint and auto-fix

## Conventions
- Named exports only
- Components use PascalCase files

## Gotchas
- Never edit src/generated/; run pnpm codegen
- E2E tests need the API on :4000

theory.title: Edit with /memory
theory.body: Caught yourself repeating an instruction? Turn it into memory: run `/memory`, pick the project or user file, add one short specific line, and save. Future sessions load it automatically.

theory.title: Or ask Claude to update it
theory.body: You can also ask Claude to edit `@CLAUDE.md` for you. Use the five prompt parts: **context** (what you keep repeating), **goal** (what to add), **constraints** (`keep each entry to one line`), **done when**, and **@ file references**.
theory.code:
I keep telling you we use pnpm. Update @CLAUDE.md:
under Commands add 'pnpm test'. Keep it to one line.
Done when that line is there and nothing else changed.

exercises.prompt: Which line is the WORST fit for CLAUDE.md?
options: Run a single test: pnpm vitest run path/to/file
Never edit files in src/generated/; run pnpm codegen
The full text of every source file
Use zod for all request validation
exercises.explanation: Claude can read the code itself; dumping it into memory wastes context every session.

exercises.prompt: Classify each CLAUDE.md line.

pairs.left: E2E tests need the API on :4000

exercises.explanation: Sorting lines into commands, conventions and gotchas shows whether each one tells Claude something it couldn't see in the code.

exercises.prompt: Why keep CLAUDE.md concise?
options: It's loaded into context every session, so every line has a cost
exercises.explanation: Memory is always in context, so lean files leave more room for the actual task.

exercises.prompt: Which gotcha entry will actually prevent a mistake?
options: Never run `pnpm db:reset` without `--env=local`; it targets staging by default.
exercises.explanation: A precise rule with the reason is something Claude can act on.

exercises.prompt: Finish this CLAUDE.md skeleton.
exercises.code:
## ___
- pnpm test: unit tests

## ___
- Named exports only

## ___
- Never edit src/generated/
exercises.explanation: Grouping lines under Commands, Conventions and Gotchas keeps memory scannable for you and Claude.
exercises.hint: The three headings are the three kinds of high-signal content: Commands, Conventions, Gotchas.

exercises.prompt: Order the habit loop for keeping memory fresh.
steps: Pick the project or user memory file
Save; future sessions load it automatically
exercises.explanation: Turning repetition into memory is how CLAUDE.md grows into something valuable.

exercises.prompt: Inside the session, type the slash command that opens your memory files for editing.
exercises.hint: / + the word for what CLAUDE.md is: /mem…
exercises.explanation: /memory opens a loaded memory file in your editor, which is the quickest way to save an instruction for good.

exercises.scenario: For the third session in a row you've had to tell Claude that your monorepo uses pnpm workspaces, that API tests need `docker compose up db`, and that files in packages/sdk/generated/ are auto-generated. Ask Claude to capture this in project memory.
exercises.sample: For three sessions I've had to repeat these, so add them to project memory. Update @CLAUDE.md: under Commands, 'pnpm -r test' runs all workspace tests and API tests need 'docker compose up db' first (see @docker-compose.yml); under Gotchas, never edit packages/sdk/generated/, regenerate with 'pnpm codegen'. Keep each entry to one line and don't change other sections. Done when those three lines are in CLAUDE.md.
exercises.explanation: Turning repeated corrections into short, specific CLAUDE.md lines means you never type them again.

mission.title: Memory Keeper
mission.intro: Give a real project a memory that makes every future session smarter.
checklist: Run /init in a real project and read the generated CLAUDE.md
Add at least one command, one convention, and one gotcha that /init missed
Start a new session and ask Claude how to run the tests to confirm it remembers
Use /memory to open and tweak one of the files
mission.explanation: With project and user memory in place, Claude starts every session already briefed.
